facts: Rudinger, White, and Van Durme authored a paper on neural models for determining factuality in text.
The research was conducted at Johns Hopkins University and the University of Rochester.
The models developed aim to assess whether statements are factual.
The work contributes to natural language processing and computational linguistics.
The paper introduces two neural models for predicting event factuality.
The models outperform prior approaches on three datasets: FactBank, UW, and MEANTIME.
The authors expand the "It Happened" component of the Universal Decompositional Semantics dataset.
The extended dataset is the largest event factuality dataset available.
The paper addresses event factuality prediction (EFP).
The authors present two neural models that outperform previous systems across four datasets.
UDS-IH2 is introduced as an extension of UDS-IH1.
The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of multi-task training and ensembling approaches.

The text examines event factuality prediction. The authors compare bidirectional LSTMs with linear chain versus dependency tree topologies. The study evaluates four factuality datasets: FactBank, MEANTIME, UW, and UDS-IH2. Previous approaches used deterministic rule-based systems with hand-engineered lexical features.
The UDS-IH2 dataset is an extension of the UDS-IH1 event factuality dataset.
Thirty-two annotators from Amazon Mechanical Turk labeled 20,580 predicates in pairs.
The inter-annotator agreement for the UDS-IH2 dataset is 0.84 (κ=0.66).
UDS-IH2's factuality ratings are mapped to a single [-3,3] scale.
The paper presents two neural models for predicting factuality.
One model is a stacked bidirectional linear chain LSTM.
The other model is a stacked bidirectional child-sum dependency tree LSTM.
Both models use a two-layer regression model to predict the factuality of an event.
The stacked bidirectional linear LSTM (L-biLSTM) extends standard LSTMs with multiple layers and bidirectional processing.
The stacked bidirectional tree LSTM (T-biLSTM) incorporates dependency tree structure for upward and downward computation.
A regression model using Huber loss takes the final hidden states as input to predict factuality scores.
The T-biLSTM omits dependency labels to maintain architectural simplicity and reduce parameters.
The authors implement L-biLSTM and T-biLSTM models in PyTorch.
They use 300-dimensional GloVe word embeddings with 300-dimensional hidden states.
Five training regimes tested include single-task specific and multi-task balanced.
Models are evaluated on FactBank, UW, MEANTIME, and UDS-IH2 datasets.
The 2-layer biLSTM variants include L-biLSTM, T-biLSTM, and H-biLSTM.
Linear topology (L-biLSTM) consistently outperforms tree topology (T-biLSTM).
The hybrid topology (H-biLSTM) achieves the best correlation on the UW dataset.
Lexical features yield minimal improvements, with slight gains only on UW.
Events without direct modals or negation have the highest average factuality.
Future events marked with "will" show the most negative factuality scores.
Manual error analysis of 50 high-error predictions reveals challenges from grammatical errors and informal language.
Linguistically-motivated lexical features show minimal overall impact on performance.
The authors propose two neural models for event factuality prediction: L-biLSTM and T-biLSTM.
L-biLSTM generally performs better than T-biLSTM.
The authors created UDS-IH2, the largest publicly-available factuality dataset to date.
The research was supported by JHU HLT-COE, DARPA LORELEI, DARPA AIDA, and NSF-GRFP.
The dataset filtering removes low-agreement annotators using two approaches.
One annotator and 4,179 annotations were removed during the filtering process.
The filtering for the HAPPENED question uses a z-scored BLUP threshold of -2.
Table 10 presents full experimental results across multiple models and variants.
